faq.q: Can you do the NC500 on an A2 bike?
faq.a: Absolutely. I've ridden the NC500 on A2-restricted bikes and the power limitation is never an issue. The roads rarely allow speeds over 60mph, and the lighter weight actually makes A2 bikes more enjoyable through the twisty sections.

faq.q: What's the best A2 touring bike for beginners?
faq.a: The Honda CB500X is my top recommendation for new tourers. It's reliable, comfortable, economical, and the low seat height builds confidence. The Kawasaki Versys 650 is a close second if you want more long-distance comfort.

faq.q: How much luggage can an A2 touring bike carry?
faq.a: Most A2 touring bikes handle 40-50kg of luggage without issues. I regularly tour with full panniers and a tail bag on my Versys. Just adjust your rear preload properly and you'll be fine.

faq.q: Are A2 bikes powerful enough for motorway touring?
faq.a: Yes, comfortably. A2 bikes sit at 70mph all day without struggling. Overtaking takes slightly more planning than on unrestricted bikes, but it's perfectly safe and practical for motorway miles.

faq.q: What fuel range should I expect from an A2 touring bike?
faq.a: Most A2 touring bikes achieve 200-250 mile range. The Honda CB500X and Kawasaki Versys regularly hit 200+ miles on a tank, while the Royal Enfield Himalayan manages around 180 miles. This is plenty for UK touring.

faq.q: Do I need to restrict a full-power bike or buy an A2 model?
faq.a: Either works, but factory A2 models or professionally restricted bikes are safer legally. Make sure any restriction is done properly with a certificate, as police and insurers will check. Bikes like the CB500X are naturally A2-compliant.

content:
Best A2 Touring Bikes for UK Adventures in 2026

Right, let's talk A2 touring bikes. If you're restricted to the A2 licence (47bhp limit), you might think proper touring is off the cards. I'm here to tell you that's rubbish. I've seen A2 riders tackle the NC500, cross to the islands, and cover more miles than plenty of unrestricted riders. The key is choosing the right bike for the job.

I've spent years riding across Britain in all weathers, and I've tested quite a few A2-compliant machines on everything from the M6 in horizontal rain to the single-track roads of Skye. What I've learned is this: for touring, comfort and reliability beat raw power every single time. And with modern A2 bikes, you're not compromising nearly as much as you might think.

What Makes a Good A2 Touring Bike?

Before we dive into specific models, let me break down what you actually need for touring on an A2 bike. I've made the mistakes so you don't have to.

The Non-Negotiables

First up: weather protection. Britain doesn't do predictable weather, and you need a bike that'll shield you from the worst of it. A decent screen and fairing make the difference between arriving knackered after three hours or feeling fresh enough to crack on for another hundred miles. I learned this the hard way riding a naked bike to Fort William in February.

Second: luggage capacity. Soft luggage works, but panniers are king for serious touring. You want a bike that either comes with hard luggage or has proper mounting points. Bungee cords and rucksacks are fine for a weekend blast, but a week in Scotland demands better organisation.

Third: fuel range. Nothing worse than fuel anxiety on the A82 between Tyndrum and Glencoe when you're not sure if the next petrol station is open. I look for tanks that'll give you 200 miles minimum, preferably more. With A2 bikes being relatively efficient, this is actually easier to achieve than you'd think.

Comfort Over Distance

Seat comfort isn't sexy, but after four hours in the saddle heading up to the Highlands, your backside will thank you for choosing wisely. Same goes for riding position. You want something upright enough that you're not putting weight on your wrists, but not so sit-up-and-beg that you catch every gust of wind like a sail.

Suspension quality matters more than you'd expect. The A9 through Perthshire will shake a budget bike to bits, and Welsh B-roads can be properly rough. Decent suspension means you arrive without feeling like you've done ten rounds with a heavyweight.

Top A2 Touring Bikes I'd Actually Recommend

These are bikes I've either ridden extensively or seen perform brilliantly in the hands of riders I trust. I'm not listing every A2 bike under the sun – just the ones that'll genuinely work for UK touring.

Kawasaki Versys 650 (A2 Restricted)

I've ridden a Versys from Land's End to John o' Groats, and it's the bike I point most A2 riders toward. It's been restricted from the factory or can be easily restricted, and even at 47bhp it's got enough grunt for motorway work and hill climbs.

The riding position is spot-on for long days, the screen is adjustable (essential for finding that sweet spot where the buffeting stops), and there's a proper luggage ecosystem available. I've had mine loaded with 40kg of camping gear and it didn't complain once.

Fuel economy is brilliant – I regularly see 60mpg, which means you can do the NC500 with minimal fuel stops. The seat gets a bit firm after 200 miles, but that's fixable with an aftermarket option from SportsBikeShop.

Suzuki V-Strom 650 (A2 Version)

The V-Strom is the sensible choice, which sounds boring until you're 300 miles into a ride and everything just works. It's comfortable, reliable as sunrise, and carries luggage like it's not even there.

I took one through the Lake District in absolutely biblical rain last year, and the combination of decent weather protection and confidence-inspiring handling made it far less grim than it could've been. The engine's got that V-twin character that makes puttering through villages pleasant rather than feeling like you're strangling a sports bike.

Suzuki's build quality is solid, and parts are readily available. The aftermarket support is excellent too – you can spec one out with everything from heated grips to fog lights. The only downside is it's not the prettiest bike in the world, but when you're watching the sun rise over Loch Lomond, you won't care.

Honda CB500X

Honda's parallel twin is smooth, economical, and utterly unbreakable. I know riders who've put 50,000 miles on these with nothing but routine maintenance. For touring, that reliability is worth its weight in gold.

The X model gives you that adventure bike stance with decent ground clearance for rougher roads. I've used one exploring the forest tracks around Kielder and it handled everything I threw at it. The 17-litre tank means 200+ mile range easily, and the fuel economy can hit 70mpg if you're gentle.

It's not exciting, I'll be honest. But boring is exactly what you want when you're planning a Island to Highlands tour. You want something that starts every morning, doesn't strand you in Ullapool, and gets you home without drama.

The best touring bike is the one that makes you want to ride it every weekend, not the one that looks best in photos. Choose comfort and reliability over specs and bragging rights.

Royal Enfield Himalayan

Bit of a wildcard, this one. It's already A2 compliant at 24bhp, and while that sounds pathetic on paper, it's perfectly adequate for touring. I've ridden one through the Cairngorms and across to Skye, and the lack of power was never an issue.

What it lacks in speed, it makes up for in character and capability. The upright position is brilliant for all-day comfort, and it'll handle terrible road surfaces without complaint. British B-roads are its happy place.

The downside is motorway work. It'll do 70mph, but it's working hard. If your touring involves lots of motorway slogs, look elsewhere. But for exploring the Welsh valleys or meandering through the Scottish Borders, it's properly enjoyable. Plus it's cheap to buy, cheap to run, and simple to maintain.

Yamaha Tracer 7 (A2 Restricted)

The Tracer 7 is basically a sports tourer in A2 clothing. Even restricted, it's got enough poke to make overtakes clean and motorway speeds relaxed. I tested one on a run up to Edinburgh via the A68 and it was cracking.

The aerodynamics are properly thought-out, the electronics are modern and useful (not just gimmicks), and the build quality feels a step above some competitors. The riding position splits the difference between sporty and touring nicely.

Luggage options are available from Yamaha and aftermarket suppliers. The only thing I'd change is the screen – it could be taller for proper motorway protection. But that's an easy fix.

What to Actually Look For When Buying

If you're buying used (which most A2 riders are), here's what I check before handing over cash.

Service History

Non-negotiable. A bike that's been serviced properly will outlast one that's been neglected by years. I always check for evidence of valve clearances being done – it's the service that separates conscientious owners from cowboys.

Tyres and Brake Pads

Check the tyres properly. Touring bikes eat through rear tyres, and good rubber isn't cheap. If the bike's wearing budget ditchfinders, that tells you something about how the previous owner maintained it. Same with brake pads – if they're worn down to nothing, walk away or negotiate hard.

Luggage Mounting Points

If touring is your goal, check the luggage mounting points haven't been bodged or damaged. I've seen bikes where someone's overtightened pannier racks and cracked mounting tabs. Fixing that is expensive and annoying.

Setting Up Your A2 Bike for Touring

Right, you've bought the bike. Now let's make it actually work for touring.

Essential Additions

First thing I fit to any touring bike is heated grips. British weather means you'll be riding in the cold, and cold hands are miserable and dangerous. Proper heated grips from SportsBikeShop are worth every penny compared to cheap alternatives that fail after one winter.

USB charging is essential unless you enjoy running out of phone battery halfway through a route. I hardwire mine in rather than using cigarette lighter adapters – more reliable and tidier. Your phone is your navigation, communication, and camera, so keep it charged.

Crashbars or engine protection is worth considering. I've dropped bikes on greasy Highland car parks more times than I'd like to admit. Crashbars mean a dropped bike is embarrassing rather than expensive.

Luggage Setup

Hard panniers are the gold standard. They're weatherproof, secure, and keep the weight low. Givi and SW-Motech make excellent options for most A2 touring bikes. Make sure whatever you buy is properly fitted – badly mounted luggage can affect handling.

A tank bag is brilliant for stuff you need access to while riding: snacks, wallet, phone if you're not using it for navigation. Magnetic ones are convenient but check they don't interfere with fuel caps on plastic-tanked bikes.

Before any big trip, use our packing checklist to make sure you've not forgotten anything crucial. I once rode to Fort William and realised I'd forgotten my wallet. That was a fun phone call.

Suspension Adjustment

If you're carrying luggage and camping gear, adjust your preload. Most touring bikes have adjustable rear suspension – use it. Too soft and the bike wallows, too stiff and you'll feel every bump. Get it right and the bike transforms.

Riding an A2 Bike on UK Tours

Let's address the elephant in the room: yes, you'll be slower than unrestricted bikes. No, that doesn't matter.

Motorway Riding

A2 bikes will sit at 70mph all day without drama. Yes, overtaking lorries takes a bit more planning, but it's perfectly doable. The key is maintaining momentum – don't brake unnecessarily and you'll find the power deficit rarely matters.

I've ridden A2 bikes the length of the M6 and honestly, the difference between 47bhp and 75bhp is academic. You're limited to 70mph anyway, and most of the time you're sitting at 60mph in traffic.

Scottish Highlands

This is where A2 bikes actually shine. The roads are twisty, the speed limits are 60mph or less, and you're rarely in a hurry. The A87 to Skye, the Bealach na Bà, the roads around Applecross – all brilliant on an A2 bike.

The lighter weight compared to full-fat adventure bikes makes them more chuckable through the twisties, and lower power means you're less likely to get yourself in trouble on damp Highland roads (which is all of them).

Welsh Roads

Wales is A2 touring paradise. The Evo Triangle, the Elan Valley, the roads through Snowdonia – all perfect for bikes with 47bhp. You'll be grinning from ear to ear and never wishing for more power.

Real-World Touring Costs

Let's talk money, because touring isn't free and A2 riders are often on tighter budgets.

Fuel costs on most A2 touring bikes work out to roughly £10-12 per 100 miles at current prices. The Versys and CB500X are at the economical end, the Tracer 7 slightly thirstier. Budget £50-70 in fuel for a 500-mile weekend tour.

Tyres last 5,000-8,000 miles depending on riding style and roads. Touring bikes are easier on tyres than sports bikes. Budget £250-350 for a set of decent touring rubber fitted.

Insurance for A2 bikes is generally reasonable, especially if you're over 25 and have some no-claims bonus. Touring modifications shouldn't affect premiums much if you declare them properly.

Planning Your First A2 Touring Trip

If you've not toured before, start small. A weekend loop is plenty to learn what works and what doesn't. I recommend the Lake District or North Wales for first-timers – spectacular roads, plenty of accommodation options, and not so far that you're committed to misery if something goes wrong.

Use our route builder to plan something realistic. On an A2 bike carrying luggage, I reckon on averaging 40-45mph including stops. That means a 200-mile day is about 5 hours of riding, plus breaks.

Pack less than you think you need. I've toured with a complete camping setup in panniers and a tail bag, and I've toured with just a change of clothes and a toothbrush. Both worked fine. The lighter setup was more fun.

Weather Preparation

British weather is reliably unreliable. I pack for all conditions on every tour. Waterproofs that actually work are essential – cheap ones fail exactly when you need them most. I've ridden through Scottish rainstorms that would test a submarine.

Layers are your friend. I wear a base layer, mid-layer, and jacket with a removable thermal liner. That covers everything from 5°C drizzle to 25°C sunshine. You'll experience both in the same day touring Scotland.

For more detailed guidance, check out our essential touring gear guide which covers everything from helmets to luggage.

The Bottom Line on A2 Touring

Here's what I wish someone had told me when I started: an A2 licence doesn't limit your touring ambitions. I've seen A2 riders cover more ground, visit more interesting places, and have more fun than riders on 150bhp superbikes who never leave their local dual carriageway.

The bikes I've mentioned will all do proper touring. Pick the one that fits your budget, your style, and your typical routes. Then just ride it. Don't wait until you pass your full test, don't convince yourself you need more power. Get out there now.

The best bit about A2 touring bikes? They teach you to ride properly. You learn to maintain momentum, read the road ahead, and plan overtakes. These skills stay with you forever, long after you've moved on to unrestricted bikes.

Start planning your first tour today. Pick a destination, book a weekend, and go. The memories you'll make matter far more than the bhp figures on your spec sheet.
